text: 8 Lecture 8 8.1 Existence, uniqueness and basic properties of the determinant Theorem 8.1. There is a unique function det : Mn×n(F ) → F satisfying the properties in Definition 7.12. In fact, the determinant is given by det(A) = ∑ σ∈Sn sign(σ)aσ(1)1aσ(2)2 · · · aσ(n)n. This is called the Leibniz formula for determinant. Proof. Let e1, . . . , en be the standard basis of F n. By multilinearity, det(A) = det( n∑ i1=1 ai11ei . . . n∑ in=1 ainnei) = n∑ i1=1 · · · n∑ in=1 ai11ai22 . . . ainn det(ei1 . . . ein) By the alternating property, det(ei1 . . . ein) = 0 if ik = il for k ̸= l. Thus the summation is over all i1, . . . , in which are distinct. We would like to permute ei1 . . . ein to e1, . . . , en and use the fact that det I = 1. By Lemma 7.13, each swap will alter the sign of det. The question is how many swaps do we need to permute ei1 . . . ein to e1, . . . , en? Definition 8.2. A permutation of n elements is a bijective map σ : {1, . . . , n} → {1, . . . , n}. To write a permutation, we just list all its values σ(1) to σ(n). We use the one-line notation to write σ = σ(1) · · · σ(n). The set of all permutation is denoted by Sn which is called the symmetric group. There are n! = n(n − 1) · · · 1 elements in Sn. An inversion in σ is a pair of indices (i, j) such that i < j and σ(i) > σ(j). The inversion number of σ, denoted inv(σ), is the total number of inversions in σ. The sign of a permutation σ is sign(σ) = (−1)inv(σ). Example 8.3. inv(123) = 0, inv(231) = 2, inv(312) = 2, inv(213) = 1, inv(132) = 1, inv(321) = 3. Lemma 8.4. The number of adjacent swaps needed to sort σ into the identity permuta- tion in the bubble sort algorithm is inv(σ). In particular, det(eσ(1) . . . eσ(n)) = sign(σ). Proof. Given a list a1, a2, . . . , an, the bubble sort proceeds as follows: (i) For each 1 ≤ i ≤ n − 1, compare ai and ai+1. (ii) If ai > ai+1, swap them. If ai < ai+1, keep them unchanged. (iii) After one full pass through the list, the largest element “bubbles up” to the end of the list. (iv) Repeat the above passes on the first n − 1, then n − 2, . . . , elements, until no swaps occur during a pass. Consider bubble sort applied to the sequence σ(1), . . . , σ(n). We claim that each swap removes exactly one inversion. Bubble sort only swaps adjacent elements σ(k) and 43 σ(k + 1) when σ(k) > σ(k + 1). This removes the inversion (k, k + 1). We now verify that the number of other inversions remains the same. Let (i, j) ̸= (k, k + 1) be an inversion before the swap. Consider the following cases: If i < k and j > k + 1, then σ(i) and σ(j) are unchanged — the inversion remains. If i < k and j = k, the inversion becomes (i, k + 1) after the swap. If i < k and j = k + 1, it becomes (i, k). If i = k and j > k + 1, it becomes (k + 1, j). If i = k + 1 and j > k + 1, it becomes (k, j). Therefore, each swap in bubble sort decreases the total number of inversions by exactly one. Since bubble sort terminates when the sequence is sorted (i.e., has zero inversions), the total number of swaps performed is equal to the number of inversions in the original sequence. Coming back to the proof since i1, . . . , in are distinct, there is σ ∈ Sn such that ik = σ(k) for all k. Therefore det(A) = ∑ σ∈Sn aσ(1)1aσ(2)2 · · · aσ(n)n det(eσ(1) . . . eσ(n)) = ∑ σ∈Sn sign(σ)aσ(1)1aσ(2)2 · · · aσ(n)n. The above argument show that any function satisfying Definition 7.12 has to have the above expression. We now check that the function given by the expression above does satisfies Definition 7.12. (i) Fix all columns except column j. Suppose vj = ax + by. Then each entry in column j satisfies aij = axi + byi for all i = 1, . . . , n. ∑ σ∈Sn sign(σ)aσ(1)1 · · · aσ(j)j · · · aσ(n)n = ∑ σ∈Sn sign(σ)aσ(1)1 · · · (axσ(j) + byσ(j)) · · · aσ(n)n =a ∑ σ∈Sn sign(σ)aσ(1)1 · · · xσ(j) · · · aσ(n)n + b ∑ σ∈Sn sign(σ)aσ(1)1 · · · yσ(j) · · · aσ(n)n. (ii) Suppose two columns are equal: vi = vj for i ̸= j. For any σ ∈ Sn let σ′ ∈ Sn such that σ′(i) = σ(j) and σ′(j) = σ(i) and σ′(k) = σ(k) for k ̸= i, j. We have seen in the proof of Lemma 8.4 that swapping two adjacent elements in a permutation change the inversion by ±1. Since we need 2|j − i| + 1 adjacent swaps to permute σ′ to σ we have sign(σ′) = (−1)2|j−i|+1 sign(σ) = − sign(σ). Since columns i and j are equal, aσ(1)1 · · · aσ(n)n = aσ′(1)1 · · · aσ′(n)n. Thus we have sign(σ)aσ(1)1 · · · aσ(n)n + sign(σ′)aσ′(1)1 · · · aσ′(n)n =(sign(σ) + sign(σ′))aσ(1)1 · · · aσ(n)n = 0. 44 Thus the terms corresponding to σ and σ′ cancel in the sum. As every permutation σ corresponds to exactly one such pair, we have ∑ σ∈Sn sign(σ)aσ(1)1aσ(2)2 · · · aσ(n)n = 0. (iii) Recall the identity matrix I = (δij), so we have δσ(1)1δσ(2)2 · · · δσ(n)n = { 1 if σ = id 0 otherwise Only the identity permutation contributes, and sign(id) = 1, so: ∑ σ∈Sn sign(σ)δσ(1)1δσ(2)2 · · · δσ(n)n = 1. Corollary 8.6. det(Pij) = −1 det(Di(λ)) = λ det(Eij(λ)) = 1 For any A ∈ Mn×n(F ) and elementary matrix E det(AE) = det(A) det(E) Proof. Since Pij is obtained by swaping column i and j of I, we have det(Pij) = −1. Since Di(λ) is obtained by multiplying column j of I by λ, we have det(Di(λ)) = λ. Since Eij(λ) is obtained by adding λ· column i to column j of I, we have det(Eij(λ)) = 1. By Remark 6.23, multiplying elementary matrices to the right of a matrix cor- responds to performing elementary column operations. Since each elementary col- umn operation corresponds to multiplying the determinant of A by det(E), we have det(AE) = det(A) det(E). Corollary 8.7. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ) be singular. Then det(A) = 0. 45 Proof. Since rank A < n, the columns of A are linearly dependent. We write A = (v1 . . . vn). By Lemma 2.8, there is a column vk which is a linear combination of v1, . . . , vk−1 i.e. vk = a1v1 + · · · + ak−1vk−1. Thus by Lemma 7.13, adding −a1v1 − · · · − ak−1vk−1 to vk we get det(A) = det(v1 . . . vk−1, 0, vk+1 . . . vn) = 0. Proposition 8.8. Let A, B ∈ Mn×n(F ). Then det(AB) = det(A) det(B). Proof. In case B is not invertible, we have first that det(B) = 0. Next, we know that AB is not invertible by Homework 4 (ST invertible =⇒ S, T are both invertible). Hence det(AB) = 0 = det(A) det(B). We have seen in Corollary 8.6 that det(AE) = det(A) det(E) for any A ∈ Mn×n(F ) and elementary matrix E. By Corollary 7.9 for any invertible matrix B, we have B = E1 · · · Em for some elementary matrices E1, . . . , Em. Hence det(AB) = det(AE1 · · · Em−1Em) = det(AE1 · · · Em−1) det(Em) = · · · = det(A) det(E1) · · · det(Em) = det(A) det(E1 · · · Em) = det(A) det(B). Corollary 8.9. A ∈ Mn×n(F ) is invertible if and only if det(A) ̸= 0. If A is invertible, then det(A)−1 = 1 det(A) . Proof. If A is not invertible then by Corollary 8.7, det(A) = 0. If A is invertible Then A−1A = I. By Proposition 8.8, det(A) det(A−1) = det(AA−1) = det I = 1. Thus det(A) ̸= 0 and det(A−1) = 1 det(A) . Remark 8.10. This Corollary shows that computing the determinant is a good way to tell whether a matrix is invertible or not. Corollary 8.11. If B = P −1AP , then det(B) = det(A). The determinant is indepen- dent of the choice of a basis. That is if T : V → V is linear then for any bases β and γ of V , we have det([T ]β β) = det([T ]γ γ). Thus we define det(T ) = det([T ]β β). Proposition 8.12. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ). Then det(At) = det(A). Proof. If A is not invertible, then by Corollary 6.17 At is not invertible. Thus det(At) = 0 = det(A). If A is invertible then by Corollary 7.9, A = E1 · · · Em for some elementary matrices E1, . . . , Em. Note that for any elementary matrix E, Et is also an elementary matrix and det(E) = det(Et). Then det(A) = det(E1) · · · det(Em) = det(Et m) · · · det(Et 1) = det(Et m · · · Et 1) = det((E1 · · · Em) t) = det(At). Remark 8.13. Thus the properties in Definition 7.12 and Lemma 7.13 are also true for rows of A. 46 8.2 Laplace expansion Proposition 8.14. Let B ∈ M(n−1)×(n−1)(F ) and u ∈ F n−1. Then det (1 ut 0 B ) = det B. By Lemma 7.13, we can perform elementary column operations to eliminate the ut using the first column. For instance one first add −u1 multiple of column 1 to column 2 to eliminate u1 and then add −u2 multiple of column 1 to column 3 to eliminate u2 ... so on and so forth and finally add −un−1 multiple of column 1 to column n to eliminate un−1. We can express this process compactly as elementary column operation by block: one add −ut multiple of the first column ( 1 0 ) to the column ( ut B ) to get ( 0 B ) which is equivalent to the matrix multiplication ( 1 ut 0 B ) ( 1 −ut 0 I ) = ( 1 0 0 B ) . Since the determinant is invariant under add multiples of other columns to one column, we have det (1 ut 0 B ) = det ( 1 0 0 B ). We define D(B) = det (1 0 0 B ) . Clearly, this function satisfies the properties in Definition 7.12 since det does. Therefore, by the uniqueness of the determinant function, it must be D(B) = det(B). Remark 8.15. A good way of computing the determinant is to use elementary row and column operations to reduce the matrix to the upper triangular form and apply the previous proposition. Remark 8.16. In the proof above, we eliminate the block ut as if it is a number that can be eliminated by the 1 in the same row. This is an efficient way to perform elementary 47 row/column operations called elementary row/column operations by blocks. A general form of it is as follows. Swap two block rows ( A21 A22 A11 A11 ) = (0 I I 0 ) ( A11 A12 A21 A22 ) . Multiply a block row by a square matrix Λ from the left: ( ΛA11 ΛA12 A21 A22 ) = ( Λ 0 0 I ) ( A11 A12 A21 A22 ) . Add a block multiple of one block row to another ( A11 A12 A21 + M A11 A22 + M A12 ) = ( I 0 M I ) ( A11 A12 A21 A22 ) where M is a matrix of appropriate size (not necessarily invertible). This generalizes the usual row addition Ri ← Ri + cRj to the block setting. The third one is most useful in computing determinants since the determinant is unchanged under such operations. The first two will differ by the determinant of the corresponding block elementary matrix. Similarly, one can also perform elementary column operations by block. In particular adding a block multiple of one block column to another column is as follows (A11 A12 + A11M A21 A22 + A21M ) = ( A11 A12 A21 A22 ) ( I M 0 I ) where M is a matrix of appropriate size (not necessarily invertible). We note that when doing the third elementary column operations by blocks, one can only multiply M to the right of a block column while when doing elementary row operations by blocks, one can only multiply M to the left of a block row. Definition 8.17. The (i, j)-minor of A, denoted by Aij is the determinant of the (n − 1) × (n − 1) matrix obtained by deleting the i-th row and the j-th column of A. The cofactor matrix Cof(A) is the matrix with entries Cof(A)ij = (−1)i+jAij. Example 8.18. If A = ( a b c d ) then Cof(A) = ( d −c −b a ). Theorem 8.19 (Laplace’s expansion formula). Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ). Then for any j = 1, . . . , n det(A) = n∑ i=1(−1) i+jaijAij = n∑ i=1(−1) i+jajiAji. 48 Proof. Let e1, . . . , en be the standard basis of F n. By multilinearity, det(A) = det(v1 . . . n∑ i=1 aijei . . . vn) = n∑ i=1 aij det(v1 . . . ei . . . vn) where ei is in the j-th column. We first do adjacent column swaps to make ei appear in the first column and then do adjacent row swaps to make the entry 1 in ei appear in the first row. Then we made i − 1 + j − 1 = i + j − 2 adjacent swaps and hence the determinant change by a factor (−1)i+j−2 = (−1)i+j. We apply Proposition 8.14 to see that det(v1 . . . ei . . . vn) = (−1)i+jAij The second equality follows from applying the formula to At and use Proposition 8.12. Definition 8.20.
